report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that giving children more vaccines causes autism is not supported by credible evidence.

The concern partly arose because autism signs are often recognized during the same early-childhood period when several vaccines are given; timing alone cannot show causation. It was amplified by a 1998 report suggesting an MMR–autism connection, but that small case series was retracted by *The Lancet*. https://www.bmj.com/content/340/bmj.c696.extract?papetoc=

Research has tested the “too many vaccines” version directly, not only MMR. A case-control study used immunization records and estimated each child’s cumulative exposure to vaccine antigens in the first two years. It found no association between greater antigen exposure—including exposure on a single day—and autism spectrum disorder. https://www.jpeds.com/article/s0022-3476(13)00144-3/fulltext

A 2014 meta-analysis combining five cohort studies and five case-control studies concluded that vaccination was not associated with autism or autism-spectrum disorder; its findings also did not support associations for MMR or thimerosal/mercury exposure. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24814559/

Large registry research likewise found no MMR association: a Danish nationwide cohort linked vaccination, autism diagnoses, other vaccines, family history, and relevant risk factors. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30831578/

No individual observational study can establish that a risk is literally zero in every conceivable subgroup. But the best available evidence—across large cohorts, pooled analyses, and direct measures of cumulative vaccine-antigen exposure—does not show that increasing the number of childhood vaccines increases autism risk.
